ECE 6390 / Orbits and look angles

Two-burn transfer

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows why a transfer to a higher circular orbit uses separate departure and circularization burns.

For circular coplanar starting and ending orbits with radii r₁ and r₂, the transfer ellipse has semimajor axis aₜ = (r₁ + r₂)/2. The first prograde impulse raises the opposite apsis.

Use vis-viva, v² = μ(2/r − 1/aₜ), to find transfer speeds at each endpoint. Compare each with the circular speed √(μ/r) at that same radius to calculate the burn magnitude.

At transfer apogee, the spacecraft reaches the correct radius but moves more slowly than the desired outer circular orbit. The second prograde burn circularizes it. Coast time is half the transfer period: π√(aₜ³/μ).

Example

For r₂ = 2r₁, the ideal total Δv is approximately 0.2845 times the initial circular speed. The two burn magnitudes are different.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. Why does a spacecraft at the transfer ellipse's apogee fall back inward if it skips the circularization burn?

    Reaching a radius and having the circular speed there are separate conditions.

    Its existing energy and angular momentum still describe the transfer ellipse. Its apogee tangential speed is below the circular speed at that radius, so gravity carries it back toward perigee.
